docs.title: Optimizer
docs.text:
optimizer.name is OptunaOptimizer or GradientDescentOptimizer.

OptunaOptimizer's settings are multi_objective, sampler (tpe, cmaes, random, simulated_annealing), pruner and random_seed (default -1, no seed). A seed makes the run repeatable when parallel_trials is 1; it reaches the tpe, cmaes and random samplers, and an optunahub sampler that accepts a seed.

cmaes is Optuna's CMA-ES sampler in its margin variant, for parameters on a step grid. It suits continuous circuit values and many parallel trials, and needs multi_objective off and more than one parameter.

"optimizer": {"name": "OptunaOptimizer", "settings": {"sampler": "tpe", "random_seed": 42}}

GradientDescentOptimizer refines a design locally, one trial at a time (parallel_trials must be 1). Its settings are learning_rate (first step as a fraction of each parameter's range, default 0.2; later steps shrink), exploration_scale (distance of its gradient probes: 1 probes at 10 % of the range, default 0.5) and random_seed. Give it a start point with the parameters' initial_value; otherwise it starts in the middle of the ranges.

"optimizer": {"name": "GradientDescentOptimizer", "settings": {"learning_rate": 0.05}}

When no trial meets every goal, the run ends at the trial that misses them by the least; over-fulfilling other goals does not count. The first trial that meets every goal often meets one of them by a hair, so tighten the bounds by the margin you want.

docs.title: Simulator
docs.text:
simulator.name is XyceSimulator (default) or VacaskSimulator. Goals whose analysis the chosen simulator cannot run are rejected before the run starts.

Simulator Setting Default Meaning XyceSimulator xyce_command, parallel_xyce, parallel_xyce_processes, enforce_passivity — Xyce executable, MPI ranks, passivity VacaskSimulator vacask_command "vacask" Command name or absolute path vacask_threads 1 vacask -n N; 0 = auto (OMP_NUM_THREADS); keep 1 with parallel_trials above 1 vector_fit_max_order 12 Highest model order snp2le may use when it fits a surrogate (integer, at least 2) enforce_passivity false Enforce passivity on the vector fit surrogate_thermal_noise false Add the surrogates' thermal noise to noise analyses; requires enforce_passivity force_dc_pin true Pin each surrogate fit to its 0 Hz point also where snp2le skips the pin for passivity below the band

Both take simulation_timeout (default 0, no limit): the seconds one simulation may run before it is stopped and the trial counts as failed. Set it well above a normal run; harmonic balance can take minutes.

See Surrogate file for the VACASK fit settings.

VACASK netlists use VACASK analysis names as simulation_parameters keys ("AC", "HB", "TRAN", "NOISE", "HBNOISE") and VACASK parameter names (from, to, points, freq, nharm, ...). Xyce keys keep their leading dot (".AC"). See VACASK Simulator.

"simulator": {"name": "VacaskSimulator", "settings": {"vacask_command": "vacask", "vacask_threads": 1, "vector_fit_max_order": 12}},
"simulation_parameters": {"AC": {"points": "500", "from": "1G", "to": "200G"}}

A component_models key is normally an instance (X1). With either simulator it may instead name a subcircuit defined in the netlist or an included file; COBRA then replaces every instance of it, at any depth, by the surrogate, whose ports are the subcircuit's pins in order. See VACASK Simulator.

"component_models": {"ISM_le_new": "../models/ism.onnx"}

docs.title: Optimization Parameters
docs.text:
Field Meaning type model_input (a geometry input of an ONNX surrogate) or netlist_variable (an element value or instance parameter in the netlist) name <component>:<onnx input> for model_input, e.g. X1:width; an element (C1) or <instance>:<parameter> (Xq1:Nx) for netlist_variable. cobra parse lists both min_value, max_value Search bounds. Keep model_input bounds inside the range the model was trained on (its input_parameter_ranges metadata); the surrogate extrapolates outside it, and cobra parse warns step Grid the values snap to; null for continuous unit Scale suffix appended verbatim to netlist_variable values: "p" writes 1.5 as 1.5p. null for model_input. VACASK prefixes are case-sensitive: use "f", not "F", for femto (cobra parse warns) linked_to Name of another parameter this one mirrors, e.g. for symmetric windings. Links must not form a cycle. A netlist_variable linked to a model_input needs its own unit, e.g. "u" initial_value Optional value the optimizer evaluates first, e.g. a known design to retune: Optuna's first trial uses it (parameters without one are sampled), gradient descent starts there. Must lie within the bounds and on the step grid; a linked parameter takes its master's

A model may declare that an input only takes values on a grid, such as whole turns. cobra parse then warns when a model_input parameter's step and min_value allow values off that grid: the model never saw them, and EM fine-tuning would round them to a different geometry.

{"name": "C5", "type": "netlist_variable", "min_value": 300, "max_value": 400, "step": 1, "unit": "f", "initial_value": 377}

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
Every goal needs a parameter, a kind, and at least one of min_value and max_value. weight (default 1.0, must be positive) sets its share of the penalty. A goal's penalty is the mean, over the points of its frequency range, of the squared miss of its bound divided by scale. Without scale the miss is relative to the bound (a miss of 1 dB at −10 dB counts as 0.1), or measured in units of 1 for a bound of 0, such as a conversion gain of at least 0 dB. Give scale (must be positive), for example 1.0 for dB goals, to measure every goal of a run in the same unit.

frequency_range is a single frequency ("130GHz", the nearest point or spectral line) or a band ("125-135GHz", every point or line inside counts); null uses the whole sweep.

kind parameter Also required catalogue An .AC parameter: an S-parameter such as S21_dB, Lp/Ls (nH), Rp/Rs (Ω), Qp/Qs, k, SRF (GHz) or K; also NF (small-signal noise, Xyce and VACASK) and, with VACASK, NF_SSB, NF_DSB (hbnoise), in dB — power_dbm Power_dBm[<node>] node gain_db Gain_dB[<port>@<node>] node; port, a driven port; source_amplitude, its SIN amplitude in volts; impedance, its z0 isolation_db Isolation_dB[<node>] node; frequency_range, naming the wanted line expression a name of your choice, e.g. Compression_dB expression, a formula; terms, its variables and the goal parameters they stand for

NF is the small-signal noise figure referred to the input port at 290 K. Both simulators run it; the mixer goals NF_SSB and NF_DSB need VacaskSimulator (see VACASK Simulator). With Xyce, COBRA adds .NOISE V(<out>) <port> ... and .PRINT NOISE format=csv ONOISE INOISE when the netlist has no .NOISE. Set the output node in simulation_parameters:

"simulation_parameters": {".NOISE": {"out": "Out", "in": "P1"}}

in defaults to port 1 and must be a P port. Without start_freq/stop_freq the sweep spans the frequencies of the NF goals. For the noise run COBRA sets the input port to AC 1 and every other AC magnitude to 0. The output port is left out of the noise figure. Surrogates are noiseless in both simulators, unless VACASK's surrogate_thermal_noise is on.

node must be a probe node and port a port of the netlist, spelled exactly as cobra parse lists them: names are case-sensitive, so OUT and Out differ.

The spectrum goals (power_dbm, gain_db, isolation_db) name the analysis they read in analysis: "HB" (the default) or "TRAN", in which case the parameter name carries a TRAN: prefix, e.g. TRAN:Power_dBm[Out]. An isolation goal's value is the margin in dB down to the strongest other line in the spectrum, DC excluded. See Harmonic Balance and Transient.

docs.title: Analysis Variants
docs.text:
analysis_variants runs an analysis again with other netlist values, e.g. HB at another drive. Each names an analysis type (AC, HB, TRAN, DC, NOISE or HBNOISE) and the netlist_values to set, named like netlist_variable parameters: an element ("R1") or "<instance>:<parameter>" ("vp_rf:ampl", a VACASK sine source's amplitude in volts). A variant name is an identifier other than an analysis type.

"analysis_variants": [
  {"name": "HB_m40", "analysis": "HB", "netlist_values": {"vp_rf:ampl": 0.00632}},
  {"name": "HB_m15", "analysis": "HB", "netlist_values": {"vp_rf:ampl": 0.112}}
]

A goal reads a variant by naming it in analysis, and its parameter takes the variant's name as a prefix: HB_m40:Power_dBm[Vdd], HB_m15:Gain_dB[vp_rf@Out], or a catalogue goal such as AC_cold:S21_dB on an AC variant. The variant runs with its type's simulation_parameters. A gain goal on a variant refers to the amplitude the variant sets for its port (<port>:ampl); its source_amplitude must be that amplitude. Each variant is one more simulation per trial. In a VACASK netlist, an alter in the control block that sets the same value later wins over the variant.

Typical uses: the supply power at the operating point (Power_dBm[Vdd] at 0-0.1GHz on a low-drive HB variant) next to the gain at the nominal drive, or the gain at a test drive for compression.

docs.title: Expression Goals
docs.text:
An expression goal bounds a formula over the values of other goals. terms maps each variable of the expression to the parameter of another goal in the configuration; that goal keeps its own bounds (give it a loose one when only the expression matters). Every term is read at the expression goal's own frequency_range, and the formula is applied elementwise. The goal's parameter is a name of your choice, unique among the goals, so that other expressions can use it as a term: expressions chain, as long as none depends on itself.

The formula takes numbers, the variables, + - * / **, and the functions abs, sqrt, exp, ln, log10, and min/max of two or more values (elementwise). Terms from several analyses need a single frequency, since their frequency points need not match. A trial missing an analysis a term reads, or whose formula gives no finite value (e.g. ln of a negative number), fails the goal like any other.

Gain compression at a test drive, the gain at the netlist's drive minus the gain on a high-drive variant, at most 1 dB, and the same relative to the gain:

{"parameter": "Compression_dB", "kind": "expression", "expression": "g - g_test",
 "terms": {"g": "Gain_dB[vp_rf@Out]", "g_test": "HB_m15:Gain_dB[vp_rf@Out]"},
 "frequency_range": "35GHz", "max_value": 1.0}

{"parameter": "Compression_pct", "kind": "expression", "expression": "100 * c / g",
 "terms": {"c": "Compression_dB", "g": "Gain_dB[vp_rf@Out]"},
 "frequency_range": "35GHz", "max_value": 10.0}

docs.title: Parallel Trials
docs.text:
parallel_trials (default 1) is the number of trials evaluated at the same time, each with its own single-threaded simulation. For small and medium-sized circuits it shortens a run more than MPI ranks (parallel_xyce); do not combine the two unless the machine has cores for both.

  • The optimizer must support it: Optuna does, gradient descent does not.
  • Trials already running when the goals are met are still finished.
  • The surrogates are fitted in that many worker processes. A Python script must therefore start the run under if __name__ == "__main__":.
  • Stage percentages in the summary are shares of the summed stage times, which exceed the wall time when trials ran concurrently.

A component whose S-parameters are the same as in an earlier trial is not fitted again, e.g. a Touchstone component or a geometry the optimizer returns to. The log gives the number of fits made and reused.

docs.title: Fine-Tuning
docs.text:
Field Default Meaning enabled false Verify the result with Palace palace_command "palace" Command that runs Palace palace_processes number of cores MPI ranks per EM simulation. Like parallel_xyce_processes, it defaults to the machine writing the configuration, so set it explicitly when sharing one iterations 3 Number of EM iterations optimizer "reuse" "reuse" or "gradient_descent" retune_trials, retune_range, retune_min_steps 0 (off), 0.3, 2 Budget and ranges of the retune geometries {} ORCA geometry per ONNX component: a preset from orca.geometry.presets or a class in a Python file

ORCA is imported only when an enabled configuration needs a geometry.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Unknown fields, unsupported schema versions or backends, broken linked-parameter references, unavailable analysis-point nodes or ports, and missing input files are rejected before optimization starts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: COBRA includes runnable assets in the examples/ folder.

docs.title: Main Script Example
docs.text:
examples/main.py demonstrates a mixed-source optimization setup.

It includes:

  • ONNX surrogate mapping for one component,
  • fixed SNP mapping for another component,
  • model-input and netlist-variable optimization,
  • linked netlist variable constraints,
  • optional ORCA geometry integration for fine-tuning-ready workflows.

docs.title: LNA With an Inductor Surrogate
docs.text:
examples/configs/lna_inductor_config.json optimizes a 130 GHz cascode LNA (examples/netlists/LNA/lna_inductor.cir, IHP SG13G2, Xyce) whose output inductor is the ORCA octagonal-inductor surrogate models/DavidL-11/inductor_octa. It tunes the inductor geometry (turns, width, space, diameter), the transistor sizes and the matching network for S11, S22, S21 and the noise figure at 125–135 GHz, keeping the amplifier stable (mu ≥ 1 from 110 to 170 GHz):

cobra parse examples/configs/lna_inductor_config.json
cobra run examples/configs/lna_inductor_config.json

The netlist holds an optimized design (inductor: 2 turns, width 10.5 µm, space 3 µm, diameter 229 µm): S11 −12.2 to −11.9 dB, S21 6.7 to 7.8 dB, NF 4.79 dB at 130 GHz. Optuna samples at random, so another run may end elsewhere. It needs Xyce, the IHP PDK path in the netlist and the ONNX model from Hugging Face.

docs.title: VACASK Example
docs.text:
examples/configs/vacask_trafo_acsp.json runs the transformer example with VacaskSimulator on the native VACASK netlist examples/netlists/VACASK/trafo_acsp.sim:

cobra parse examples/configs/vacask_trafo_acsp.json
cobra run examples/configs/vacask_trafo_acsp.json

It needs vacask on PATH; see VACASK Simulator.

examples/configs/vacask_lna_trafo_hb.json optimizes the 130 GHz LNA (examples/netlists/VACASK/lna_trafo_hb.sim) for harmonic-balance gain. It uses the IHP SG13G2 PDK converted for VACASK; see PDK models.

examples/configs/vacask_lna_inductor.json is the LNA with an inductor surrogate for VACASK (examples/netlists/VACASK/lna_inductor.sim): the same circuit, parameters and goals. It sets vector_fit_max_order to 40, because the inductor model spans 0 to 500 GHz and an order-12 fit misses it by up to 0.17 in |S| at 110 to 170 GHz.

cobra parse examples/configs/vacask_lna_inductor.json
cobra run examples/configs/vacask_lna_inductor.json

docs.title: Example Data Files
docs.text:
You will find sample files such as:

  • .cir netlists
  • .onnx surrogate model files
  • .sNp Touchstone files

Tip

Start by running examples/main.py unchanged, then clone it into your own experiment script and modify one section at a time.

docs.title: Suggested Adaptation Order
docs.text:
1. Replace netlist path.
  2. Replace component mapping files.
  3. Keep design goals unchanged for first run.
  4. Expand optimization parameter ranges after baseline run succeeds.
  5. Add fine-tuning options only after surrogate-only flow works.

docs.title: Expected Artifacts
docs.text: After successful runs, compare generated files under results/ to understand how model predictions and simulation outputs evolve over iterations.

docs.title: GUI Mode
docs.text:
The COBRA GUI is launched with:

cobra

docs.title: What You Can Configure
docs.text:
The configuration panel has the sections Netlist and models, Analyses, Optimizer, Simulator and Fine-tuning. Click a title to collapse a section to a one-line summary. Rarely changed settings sit behind its Advanced fold; the Enabled box in its header switches fine-tuning on.

  • Netlist source
  • Component-to-model mapping (.onnx or .sNp). Hover over the model field to see what an ONNX model declares: its band, trained ranges, feasibility constraints and guarantees
  • Simulator: XyceSimulator or VacaskSimulator. Switching re-reads the netlist, and the goal list offers only what the simulator can run
  • Subcircuit surrogate: Use as surrogate replaces every instance of the selected subcircuit by a model (see VACASK Simulator), Clear undoes it
  • Analysis variants: further analyses of a type, each on the netlist with some values changed (e.g. the HB at another drive)
  • Design goals (S-parameter and RF metrics, and expressions over other goals)
  • Analysis point, when the run includes a Harmonic Balance or transient analysis
  • Optimization parameters and ranges
  • Iteration control and stop behavior
  • Parallelism: either N independent trials or one N-rank MPI simulation
  • Optional fine-tuning settings, including the retune after a Palace iteration that misses the goals (Retune trials, Retune range (±%), Retune min steps; see Fine-Tuning)

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: The theme button in the top-right corner cycles through system → light → dark: Sandbank (light) and Deepwater (dark), or whichever the operating system uses.

docs.title: Typical GUI Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Load Netlist] --> B[Map Components]
    B --> C[Define Design Goals]
    C --> D[Set Optimization Parameters]
    D --> E[Run Optimization]
    E --> F[Inspect Live Plots and Loss]
    F --> G[Review Saved Results]

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text:
The Parallelism row offers one choice and one process count:

  • Independent trials — the recommended mode. Processes trials are evaluated at the same time, each in its own single-core simulation. This is saved as parallel_trials.
  • Parallel simulator (MPI) — one trial at a time, each simulation on Processes MPI ranks (parallel_xyce and parallel_xyce_processes). Only worthwhile for very large netlists; it needs an MPI-enabled Xyce build.

The GUI never enables both, and rejects a configuration that does.

docs.title: Optimization Parameters
docs.text:
The parameter dialog sets a parameter's bounds, step, unit and link, and an optional Start value (initial_value): the value the optimizer evaluates first, for example a known design you want to retune. None lets the optimizer choose. For an ONNX model input, the dialog takes the bounds, and the step of an input such as whole turns, from the model's metadata.

The Optimizer row offers OptunaOptimizer (the default, a global search) and GradientDescentOptimizer, a local search that runs one trial at a time.

docs.title: Design Goals in Practice
docs.text:
Use goal constraints with optional frequency ranges, for example:

  • S11 <= -9 dB in 125-135ghz
  • -3 dB <= S21 <= 0 dB in 125-135ghz
  • Power_dBm[Out] >= 10 dB at 35ghz (single spectral line of an HB run)

The goal dialog groups the parameters by the analysis that produces them (.AC, .HB, .TRAN) in a tab bar at the top; the netlist's own analysis is opened first, and a goal from another tab adds that analysis to the run. Below, the dialog offers the inputs the selected parameter takes: choose Whole sweep / spectrum, Single frequency (the nearest frequency of the sweep or spectral line is used) or Frequency range. Goals that only make sense one way are restricted accordingly — an isolation goal, for example, has no max value and always targets a single frequency. Scale is the unit a miss of the limit is measured in (e.g. 1 for one dB); left empty, a miss counts relative to the limit, or in units of 1 for a limit of 0.

Analysis variants (the list above the goals; Add variant, right-click to edit or delete) run an analysis on the netlist with values changed: give a name, the analysis type and the values, e.g. vp_rf:ampl=0.00632, R1=60. Each variant has its own tab in the goal dialog. A variant that goals read cannot be renamed or deleted. See Analysis Variants.

The dialog's Expression tab makes a goal on a formula over other goals: name it and write the Expression with the variables listed under Terms (double-click one to insert it), e.g. a - b for compression. A goal an expression uses cannot be deleted. See Expression Goals.

Note

Goals are transformed into penalty values. Satisfying goals yields zero or negative penalty (reward), violations increase positive penalty.

docs.title: Parameter Types
docs.text:
• MODEL_INPUT: geometry/model inputs for ONNX surrogate components.
  • NETLIST_VARIABLE: parsed netlist values patched directly in netlist text.

docs.title: Models from Hugging Face
docs.text: The HuggingFace button of a component lists the models tagged orca-rfic on Hugging Face and those already downloaded ([LOCAL]). Download saves a repository to ./models/<owner>/<repo>/; Use selects its <repo>.onnx. A repository may also hold <repo>.py with the ORCA geometry class; without it, EM fine-tuning is off for that model. ORCA's documentation covers sharing your own models.

docs.title: During Optimization
docs.text:
The GUI displays:

  • live S-parameter traces,
  • the HB or transient output spectrum at the selected analysis point, as power, gain, voltage or current,
  • per-goal penalty/loss behavior,
  • current and best trial values,
  • progress against maximum iterations (the bar turns amber while paused and green when finished).

When the run ends, parameters, goals and plots show its final result: the trial that met the goals or, if none did, the one that missed them by the least.

When a run produces more than one of the S-parameter, HB and transient plots, a selector switches the left plot between them. See Advanced -> Harmonic Balance for the spectrum markers and mixing-product labels, and Advanced -> Transient Analysis for the FFT window.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Results are stored in a timestamped folder under results/ and include generated surrogate/predicted touchstone files, SPICE subcircuits, and run context.

docs.title: Script Mode
docs.text: Script mode provides full automation and reproducibility.

docs.title: Minimal Flow
docs.text:
1. Parse the netlist with XyceNetlistParser().parse_file(...), which returns a Netlist.
  2. Create COBRA with component mappings and optimizer/simulator.
  3. Define design goals.
  4. Define optimization properties.
  5. Call cobra.run(...).

docs.title: Reference Example
docs.text:
Use examples/main.py as the canonical end-to-end script.

from cobra import (
    COBRA,
    DesignGoal,
    OptimizationProperty,
    OptimizationType,
    OptunaOptimizer,
    XyceSimulator,
)
from cobra.optimizers.design_goal_collection import find_parameter
from cobra.spice_sim.netlist_parsers.xyce_netlist_parser import XyceNetlistParser

docs.title: Key Construction Pattern
docs.text:
netlist = XyceNetlistParser().parse_file("your_netlist.cir")

cobra = COBRA(
    netlist=netlist,
    component_onnx_mapping={
        "X1": "model.onnx",
        "X2": "fixed_component.s6p",
    },
    optimizer=OptunaOptimizer(multi_objective=False, sampler="tpe", pruner="median"),
    circuit_simulator=XyceSimulator(),
)

docs.title: Defining Goals and Parameters
docs.text:
A goal binds one DesignParameter to min/max limits. Look parameters up by name with find_parameter(...), or list the ones valid for a netlist with get_available_parameters(num_ports).

DesignGoalHarmonic Balance goalAnalysis variant and expressionOptimizationProperty 
goals = [
    DesignGoal(find_parameter("S11_dB"), max_value=-9, frequency_range="125-135ghz"),
    DesignGoal(find_parameter("S21_dB"), min_value=-3, max_value=0, frequency_range="125-135ghz"),
]

from cobra.optimizers.design_goal_collection import make_power_dbm

# Output power at one spectral line of an .HB run
goals.append(
    DesignGoal(make_power_dbm("Out"), min_value=10.0, frequency_range="35ghz")
)

Power and gain parameters depend on the nodes and ports of the circuit, so they are built per netlist instead of being looked up by name. See Advanced -> Harmonic Balance.

from cobra import AnalysisVariant, SimulationType
from cobra.optimizers.design_goal_collection import (
    make_expression_parameter,
    make_gain_db,
    with_variant,
)

# The HB once more, with the RF source at a test drive
test_drive = AnalysisVariant.create("HB_m15", SimulationType.HB, {"vp_rf:ampl": 0.112})
gain = make_gain_db("vp_rf", 0.0894, 100.0, "Out")
gain_at_test = with_variant(make_gain_db("vp_rf", 0.112, 100.0, "Out"), test_drive)
goals += [
    DesignGoal(gain, min_value=0.0, frequency_range="35ghz"),
    DesignGoal(gain_at_test, min_value=-100.0, frequency_range="35ghz"),
]
# Compression at the test drive: at most 1 dB
compression = make_expression_parameter("Compression_dB", "g - g_test", {"g": gain, "g_test": gain_at_test})
goals.append(DesignGoal(compression, max_value=1.0, frequency_range="35ghz"))

A goal on a variant makes each trial run that variant too, on a copy of the netlist with its values set. An expression reads its terms' analyses; a term may be another expression parameter.

params = [
    OptimizationProperty(
        name="X1:bottom_winding_diameter",
        type=OptimizationType.MODEL_INPUT,
        min_value=20.0,
        max_value=100.0,
        step=0.1,
    ),
    OptimizationProperty(
        name="Cshunt_p",
        type=OptimizationType.NETLIST_VARIABLE,
        unit="F",
        min_value=0.0,
        max_value=20.0,
        step=1.0,
    ),
]

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
context = cobra.run(
    netlist="your_netlist.cir",
    design_goals=goals,
    optimization_parameters=params,
    max_iterations=200,
    results_name="your_experiment_name",
)

run() returns an OptimizationContext, a dataclass whose fields are read as attributes. The same object is passed to callback on every iteration.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
COBRA reports progress and problems through the standard logging module, on the cobra logger tree, and installs no handlers of its own. A script sees nothing until it configures logging, either with logging.basicConfig() or with the same setup the CLI uses:

from cobra.console import configure_logging

configure_logging()                              # info level, on stderr
configure_logging(verbose=1, log_file="run.log") # debug, plus a log file

Because it is ordinary logging, an embedding application can route COBRA's output anywhere by adding its own handler to logging.getLogger("cobra").

docs.title: Optional Fine-Tuning
docs.text: You can configure optional EM fine-tuning by providing Palace command and ORCA geometry. See Advanced -> Fine-Tuning.
